files.text:
The cheapest way to Mars

Walter Hohmann was a civil engineer in the building department of the city of Essen, and he worked out the arithmetic of travel between the planets in his spare time, with tables and a slide rule, years before anyone had a rocket that could leave the ground for long. In 1925 he published it as a slim book, Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper, the attainability of the heavenly bodies. Most of it is about fuel, because fuel is what a journey in space is made of: every change of speed has to be bought with propellant carried up from the ground.

His answer for going from one circular orbit to a larger one is the curve on the plate that opened this page. Fire once, forwards, to stretch your own orbit into an ellipse whose nearest point to the Sun is where you are and whose farthest point just touches the orbit you want. Then coast, with the engine cold, for exactly half a turn of that ellipse. At the far end you are moving too slowly to stay on the bigger circle, so you fire forwards once more and you are on it. Two burns, both along the direction of travel, and nothing wasted on turning.

For Earth to Mars the half-turn takes about two hundred and fifty-nine days. The first burn adds a little under three kilometres a second to the speed Earth already gives you round the Sun; the second, at Mars's orbit, about two and a half more. Because the craft is a planet in its own right for those eight and a half months, it obeys Kepler like one: quick while it is still close to the Sun, slow as it climbs, so the first half of the journey in time carries it well over half the way round.

The catch is timing. The craft takes the long way round the Sun, and Mars has to be at the far end when it gets there, so at the moment of the first burn Mars must already be some forty-four degrees ahead of Earth in its orbit. That geometry comes round only once every two years and two months or so, which is why missions to Mars leave in clusters and why the dates are fixed long before anything is built.

Earth runs round the Sun in a year, Mars in about six hundred and eighty-seven days, so Earth gains on Mars by a little under half a degree a day and laps it every seven hundred and eighty. Each lap brings the forty-four degree lead round once, and with it a launch period of a few weeks. Miss it and the arithmetic does not care: the same two burns will be just as cheap again, twenty-six months later.

Real planets are not on circles and not quite in one plane, so real trajectories are Hohmann's ellipse bent and tilted to fit. The shape is still his. Mariner, Viking and every rover since has flown some version of the curve a city engineer drew in Essen to see whether it could be done.

# hohmann-loader A page loader drawn as an engraved plate of a Hohmann transfer from Earth to Mars. While the page loads, the transfer ellipse is inked from the departure point on Earth's orbit, over the top of the plate, to the point where it touches Mars's orbit. Earth and Mars move on their own orbits in the same time; Mars arrives at the meeting point exactly as the craft does, at 100%. Then the plate lifts off the page. No labels, no numbers, no controls. The Sun, two hairline orbits, a dotted projected course, the line being drawn, the craft at its tip, and the two planets, all in one warm ink on the house paper. A small inline variant does the same thing in a button or a sentence. ## Markup The page plate, first thing in ``, plus one line in `` so it is there from the first paint (and lifts itself after 12 s if the script never arrives): ```html
... ``` By default it follows the document: the parser finishing, every `` completing, and the `load` event. Between those it creeps forward slowly so a stalled network never looks frozen, but it never passes 92% until `load` says so. For an app that knows its own progress (fetching data, hydrating, unpacking a bundle), take it over: ```html
``` ```js const plate = document.querySelector('[data-hohmann-loader="page"]').hohmannLoader; plate.setProgress(0.4); // 0..1; it only ever draws forwards plate.done(); // finish the transfer; the plate then leaves by itself ``` The inline loader. Its `` is the source of truth: set `value` and it draws; leave `value` off and it waits in the parking orbit. ```html ``` ```js progressEl.value = 42; // or el.hohmannLoader.setProgress(0.42) el.hohmannLoader.wait(); // back to waiting (a new job) el.addEventListener('hohmann:arrive', …); // the craft has reached Mars ``` `import { hohmannLoader } from './hohmann-loader.js'` starts one by hand; it returns the same controller (`setProgress`, `done`, `wait`, `leave`, `destroy`, `progress`, `orbit`). `destroy()` stops everything and removes what it added. The page plate fires `hohmann:arrive` when the craft arrives and `hohmann:done` when it has gone; both bubble to `document`. ### Options (data attributes or the options object) | | default | | |---|---|---| | `data-hohmann-loader` | inline | `page` for the full-page plate | | `data-source` | `document` | page only: `manual` to drive it yourself | | `data-pace` | `1.25` | the shortest time, in seconds, to draw the whole transfer. A page that is ready at once still shows the arc drawn, briefly, not a flash | | `data-coast` | `2.6` | inline: seconds per parking orbit while waiting | | `data-fine` | false | inline: draw the engraved detail (Sun rays, hatched planets, ticks); for an inline loader shown large | Theme with `--paper` and `--ink`. Inline size is `--hl-size` (default 1.45em). ## The real thing Walter Hohmann, a civil engineer in Essen, published the transfer in 1925 in *Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper*. Everything on the plate follows it: - **Two circular, coplanar orbits**, Earth's at 1 AU and Mars's at 1.5237 AU, drawn to scale against each other. (The Sun and planets are not to scale; at true size they would be specks.) - **The transfer ellipse is tangent to both**: perihelion on Earth's orbit, aphelion on Mars's, so a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 and e = (r₂ − r₁)/(r₂ + r₁) = 0.2075. Both burns are along the direction of travel; the departure and the arrival are marked with a small open ring. - **The transfer takes half the ellipse's period**, t = π√(a³/μ): 258.9 days. - **Progress is time, not distance.** Progress p is mean anomaly M = πp. Kepler's equation M = E − e sin E is solved by Newton's method every frame, then ν = 2 atan2(√(1+e) sin E/2, √(1−e) cos E/2) and r = a(1 − e cos E). So the craft runs away from the Sun and slows as it climbs: at 50% of the time it is already 113° of the 180° round. The small ticks along the drawn line are cut at each tenth of the transfer time, and you can see Kepler in them: wide apart near the start, crowding together towards Mars. - **The planets keep their own time.** Earth moves at its mean motion and is 255° on by arrival. Mars must lead Earth by π − n₂t = 44.3° at departure to meet the craft; it does, and it moves at its own, slower rate to arrive at the meeting ring exactly at 100%. - **The inline loader waits for its window.** With no value it coasts: Earth (with the craft) and Mars go round at their true relative rates. When a value arrives the clock runs on, quickly and with both planets together, to the instant Mars leads by 44.3°, and the craft departs from wherever Earth then is. Nothing cheats; it is only fast-forwarded. Simplified: real orbits are slightly elliptical and inclined; burns are impulsive (all the Δv at one instant). ## The look An astronomical plate in one ink: the Sun engraved as a disc ruled with fine horizontal lines and a crown of tapering rays, long and short in turn; the planets shaded on the side away from the Sun with parallel lines that thicken towards the dark limb and begin very fine on the day side, so the terminator is soft; the drawn course a burin line that enters the plate thin and swells to full width. Each engraved mark is a filled sliver, not a stroked line, so it swells and tapers like a cut line. The orbits are true hairlines: their widths are set in CSS pixels from the plate's rendered size, so they stay 0.7 px at any size and any DPR (SVG, so sharp at any zoom). The page plate sits in a plate mark: the shallow step a copper plate presses into the sheet, lit on one side and shadowed on the other, with inside it the faint tone that wiping leaves on the plate (`assets/plate-tone.webp`, made by `scratch/hohmann-loader-p/tone.py`: long diagonal wiping streaks and paper tooth, kept to 1-3% ink). ## Behaviour and cost - **Nothing runs at rest.** The frame loop exists only while the line still has somewhere to go, while the document source is waiting on `load` (the creep), or while an inline loader is waiting on screen in a visible tab. A manual plate that is stalled draws nothing. Once the plate has left, there is no loop, no observer and no node left behind. - **Reduced motion:** no loop at all. Each change of progress redraws the plate once, with the transfer inked to exactly the current fraction and the planets in their true places; on completion the plate is removed without a fade. - **Accessible.** The page plate is a `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuenow`; the inline loader keeps its native `` for screen readers. The drawing is `aria-hidden`. - **No JS:** the `` failsafe lifts the plate after 12 s; the inline loader is the plain ``. - SVG only, about 450 lines of JS, one 110 KB texture for the page plate. ## Credits `assets/credits.json`. No outside artwork; the plate tone is generated.
